planting.note: Set divisions into wet, shaded rock crevices or a tufa wall in spring; this gesneriad needs constant moisture at the root with sharp drainage at the crown and dies back completely in winter, resprouting from a tough rhizome.

directions: Conandron ramondioides is a deciduous Japanese rock-garden gesneriad that dies back completely in winter and resprouts in spring from a thick, woody rhizome anchored into wet, shaded rock crevices. Large, soft, wrinkled, toothed leaves form a flattened rosette pressed against the rock face, and in mid to late summer it sends up branched clusters of small, star-shaped, violet-purple flowers reminiscent of a miniature Ramonda. It thrives only where roots stay constantly moist and cool while the crown stays out of standing water, traditionally grown on vertical tufa, mossy rock walls, or shaded streamside boulders in Japan, Korea, and Taiwan. Propagate by division of the rhizome or leaf-section cuttings rather than seed for best results in cultivation.

planting.note: Plant divisions in cool, consistently moist, acidic humus soil in deep shade; this Taiwanese high-elevation species resents summer heat and drying wind, so give it a sheltered, north-facing site with leaf-mold mulch.

directions: Shortia rotundifolia is a Taiwanese high-elevation evergreen groundcover in the Diapensiaceae, forming a low mat of glossy, rounded, leathery leaves similar in texture to its better-known relative Shortia uniflora. In spring it produces nodding, bell-shaped white flowers with finely fringed petal edges held just above the foliage on wiry stems. Like other Shortia species it demands cool, constantly moist, acidic humus soil and deep shade, and resents summer heat and drying winds, making it a true connoisseur's plant for shaded rock gardens in cooler climates. Propagate by careful division of established mats, since seed-grown plants are slow and demanding.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers 2-3 in deep after the soil has warmed in spring, in gritty, humus-enriched soil with good winter drainage; mark the spot since the tiny plant emerges late and goes dormant again by autumn.

directions: Roscoea tibetica is one of the smallest members of its ginger-family genus, a dwarf Himalayan and Tibetan woodland tuberous perennial that holds its orchid-like purple flowers nearly at ground level among narrow, grassy leaves only 2-4 inches tall. It emerges late in the season, often not until early summer, and goes fully dormant by autumn, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant tuber. Grow it in gritty, humus-enriched soil with reliable moisture during growth but better drainage than most woodland plants in winter, tucked into a partially shaded rock garden or woodland-edge trough where its diminutive scale will not be lost among larger neighbors. Divide dormant tubers in early spring to increase stock.

planting.note: Plant dormant tuberous roots in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil at the woodland edge; growth and flowering come later in the season than most garden roscoeas, so site it where early-season neighbors will not hide it.

directions: Roscoea wardii, collected in Tibet by plant hunter Frank Kingdon-Ward, is a taller, later-blooming relative of the more familiar garden roscoeas, producing hooded, purple-violet flowers above lance-shaped leaves in late summer. It shares the tuberous, winter-dormant habit typical of the genus, dying back completely after frost and re-emerging from below ground the following late spring. Plant it in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in dappled shade at the woodland edge, where its late flowering extends the roscoea display started earlier in the season by R. cautleyoides and R. purpurea. Increase by dividing the fleshy tuberous roots when dormant.

planting.note: Plant small tubers just below the soil surface in moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; give it a contained bed since aerial bulbils drop and self-sow readily.

directions: Pinellia cordata is a diminutive Chinese woodland aroid grown for its small, heart-shaped leaves marked with silvery veining along the midrib, forming a low, spreading carpet in shaded beds and containers. Tiny arum-type flowers consisting of a slender green spathe partly hidden by the foliage appear through summer, followed by aerial bulbils that readily drop and sprout, so give it a contained spot or expect it to wander. It prefers consistently moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade and dies back to its tuber in winter, returning reliably each spring. Divide offset tubers or collect self-sown bulbils to propagate.

planting.note: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; confine it to a bed with a root barrier or mowed edge, as self-sown bulbils spread modestly over time.

directions: Pinellia tripartita is a larger-growing relative of the more diminutive P. cordata, with distinctive three-lobed, arrow-shaped leaves and curious maroon-purple arum spathes that trail a long, thread-like appendage from the tip. Like its relatives it spreads by producing small bulbils at the leaf base that drop and self-sow, so it is best given a contained bed where its modest tendency to wander will not become a nuisance among choicer woodland neighbors. Grow in moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; the foliage dies back in winter and the tuber resprouts reliably in spring. Established clumps can be divided in early spring.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil sheltered from drying wind; this low, mounding hydrangea relative suits a shaded border or woodland garden where larger shrubs would overwhelm the space.

directions: Platycrater arguta is the sole species in its genus, a low, mounding deciduous shrub in the hydrangea family native to shaded woodlands of Japan, grown for its curious summer flowers in which the enlarged, papery, bladder-like sepals surround a small white to pale lavender true flower, giving rise to the common name bladder flower. Its soft, toothed, bright green leaves and compact habit, rarely exceeding two feet, make it a fine textural shrub for a shaded border or woodland garden where larger hydrangea relatives would overwhelm the space. It prefers consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade and benefits from shelter from drying winds. Propagate by softwood cuttings taken in early summer.

planting.note: Sow stratified seed in autumn in a deeply shaded woodland bed with humus-rich soil; most growers instead start from nursery-propagated rootstock since seed is slow and erratic to germinate.

directions: Panax japonicus is the East Asian counterpart to American ginseng, a deep-shade woodland herb known in Japanese herbal tradition as chikusetsu ninjin for its distinctive jointed, chain-like rhizome, which contrasts with the single branched taproot of P. quinquefolius. Palmately compound leaves rise on a single stem to a loose umbel of small greenish flowers followed by red berries in late summer, closely mirroring the growth habit of its American relative. Like other woodland Panax species it requires deep canopy shade, cool humus-rich soil, and years of undisturbed growth before the rhizome reaches useful size, making it a long-term planting rather than a quick crop. Stratified seed is slow and erratic to germinate, so most growers start from nursery-propagated rootstock.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; mulch well over winter at the colder end of its range, as it is less widely tested in cultivation than hardy begonia.

directions: Begonia emeiensis is a rare, cold-hardy Chinese species native to shaded ravines on Mount Emei in Sichuan, forming a low, stemless rosette of rounded, bronze-green leaves close to the ground rather than the upright cane habit of hardy begonia (B. grandis). Clusters of small pink flowers appear on short stalks in late summer, and the whole plant dies back to a dormant rhizome with the onset of cold weather, resprouting the following spring. It wants the same moist, humus-rich, part- to full-shade conditions as other woodland begonias but is less widely tested in cultivation and best given a sheltered site with reliable winter mulch outside its mildest hardiness range. Propagate by dividing the rhizome in spring as new growth begins.
